claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by surface segregation.
Elements with lower intrinsic melting temperatures preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation creates a chemically heterogeneous shell having lower cohesive energy.
The lower-cohesive-energy shell initiates premelting below the bulk melting point.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase random solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions in their cores.
Surface treatment or coating can be used to minimize surface segregation while retaining a suitable comparison with untreated nanoparticles.
The comparison will use thermally ramped in situ TEM heating and differential scanning calorimetry.
The proposed regime is approximately 5–50 nm under inert atmosphere or vacuum.
Particles in the 5–50 nm range are representative of materials used for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, and corrosion-resistant applications.
Atomic size mismatch and enthalpic driving forces cause formation of a surface layer enriched in lower-melting-point species during heating.
Local chemical composition and bonding can alter interfacial stability in an HEA-containing material.
Local bonding differences and atomic size mismatch drive lower-melting-point elements toward the free surface.
Segregation lowers local cohesive energy and therefore lowers the surface premelting-onset temperature relative to the nanoparticle core.
Particles with measurable surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements will soften or change morphology at lower temperatures than particles with homogeneous surfaces.
HEA nanoparticles with non-segregated surfaces will have a higher, more uniform melting onset that approaches the predicted bulk melting point.
The proposed segregation mechanism should hold for HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in size under inert or vacuum conditions.
The behavior may differ in bulk materials or oxidizing environments.
The magnitude of melting-point depression may depend on particle size, elemental composition, kinetic factors, and processing history.
Two sets with identical overall composition and size distribution, differing in treatment intended to suppress segregation, provide the proposed controlled comparison.
Similar premelting onsets accompanied by no significant surface-composition difference would falsify the claim that surface segregation governs the lowered premelting point.
